count.heading: How to count distinct values in a CSV column
count.text: Open the count tool on this page and load your file from disk. The browser parses the sheet without sending it to a server. The first row is treated as column headers, then pick the delimiter that matches your export: comma, semicolon, tab, or pipe. Blank lines in the file are ignored during import. Choose one column from the header list to analyze. Run the count after loading the data and choosing a column. The tool tallies how often each exact cell value appears, treats empty cells as their own category, and expresses each tally as a percentage of all rows in that column with two decimal places. The on-screen table shows a slice of the frequency list; use download to save the complete result set as CSV for sorting, filtering in another editor, or archiving.

count.heading: Worked example: category column with blanks and near-duplicates
count.text: Suppose a five-row export has header Category and rows: Apple, apple, Banana, an empty cell, and Apple again. Case and spaces matter: Apple and apple are two separate values, not one merged label. Use a second column containing a record ID so that the row with an empty Category is not a completely blank row; that empty category contributes one occurrence. Frequency output would list Apple twice (two rows), apple once, Banana once, and blank once, with shares of 40%, 20%, 20%, and 20% respectively. If you expected a single “apple” total, the result is telling you the source data used inconsistent casing rather than merging variants. Check the five data rows in the source: five is the denominator and the sum of counts equals five.

count.heading: What counts as the same value
count.text: Matching is literal text in the cell after the file is split into fields. Uppercase and lowercase letters differ, so US and us are two keys. Leading or trailing spaces inside the field are preserved, so "East " and "East" do not combine. Punctuation and internal spacing must match exactly. The tool does not trim, fold case, or normalize Unicode forms unless your source file already did. Empty cells are included in the frequency table as their own entry rather than skipped, which helps you see missing-data volume. Duplicate rows in the file each increment the same value’s count; this tool does not collapse duplicates unless you dedupe elsewhere first. If two values look identical on screen but split separately, inspect for hidden characters or delimiter misreads in the source file.

count.heading: Headers, delimiters, and quoted CSV fields
count.text: Only the first row supplies column names used in the column list; data rows start on line two. If your vendor file has title rows above headers, strip those lines before upload or counts will attach to the wrong column. European spreadsheets often use semicolon as the field separator while English ones use comma; mis-guessing merges columns and produces nonsense distinct values. Tab- and pipe-delimited logs need the matching setting so commas inside text stay inside one field. Standard double-quote wrapping allows commas, semicolons, or line breaks within a single cell; the parser respects quotes so one marketing tag with commas does not become three pseudo-values. After processing, inspect the result and compare it with a few source rows. Wrong delimiter typically shows one ultra-wide column or many empty-looking columns.

count.heading: Local processing and what you see in the UI
count.text: Parsing and aggregation run in your browser session on the machine that loaded the page. The file is not uploaded to this site for counting. That suits audits, HR extracts, and client files where policy restricts cloud tools. Very large files may feel slower or memory-bound depending on device and browser; if the tab struggles, split the source file or work on a column subset in a smaller extract first. The interface shows up to twelve frequency rows in the preview area for a quick sanity check. The download action exports every distinct value and its count and percentage, not capped at twelve. Closing the tab clears in-memory data unless you saved output. Private mode still keeps work local but offers no persistence across sessions beyond what you download.

count.heading: Reading percentages and validating the total
count.text: Each percentage is that value’s row count divided by the number of data rows in the chosen column, scaled to one hundred and shown with two decimal places. Rounding can make printed percentages sum to ninety-nine point nine nine or one hundred point zero one; compare integer counts if you need an exact audit. A dominant single value with ninety-plus percent share often means a default code, placeholder, or bulk import error. A long tail of values each at zero point zero one percent may be typos, unit variants, or free text that should be bucketed upstream. Cross-check: sum of counts across all rows in the frequency table should equal the number of non-skipped data lines for that column. If blank appears with high share, plan imputation or filter rules before modeling. Re-run on a sibling column to confirm delimiter choice stayed correct.

count.heading: When frequency tables help and sensible follow-up
count.text: Cardinality checks before joins show whether a key column is almost unique or heavily repeated. Survey and form exports benefit from seeing how often each option was chosen, including unanswered blanks. Inventory or SKU columns reveal duplicate codes versus true distinct products when you compare count output to business expectations. After counting, you might dedupe rows on a composite key if repeats explain skewed frequencies, or unpivot wide survey grids so each question becomes one column to count answers separately. For cleanup, use the frequency list to build a correction spreadsheet outside this site, then re-import. Saving the downloaded CSV gives you a stable snapshot for documentation. For keys meant to be unique, a single value with count greater than one flags dedupe candidates without manual pivot tables.

dedupe.heading: How to remove duplicate CSV rows by selected columns
dedupe.text: Load your CSV in the dedupe tool with the correct delimiter and verify the displayed column names. Blank rows in the source file are skipped on ingest. Select one or more columns that define uniqueness for your task, such as email alone or customer id plus transaction date together. The tool compares entire rows only on those fields; other columns are carried along but ignored for match decisions. When multiple data rows share the same key values under exact comparison, the earliest row in file order is kept and later matches are dropped from the output. Case and spacing in decoded key columns must match exactly for rows to be considered duplicates. Preview shows up to twelve surviving rows; download returns the full deduped CSV with the same column order as the input.

dedupe.heading: Worked example: subscription list with repeated emails
dedupe.text: Consider a file with columns email, signup_date, and source. Row two and row four both have email "user@example.com", signup_date "2024-01-10", and source "web"; row four appears later in the file. With only email selected as the key, both rows match on one column and the first occurrence (row two) is retained; row four is removed even if signup_date or source differed. If you instead select email and signup_date together, rows that share email but differ on date would both remain. A third row with "User@example.com" would not match "user@example.com" because comparison is case-sensitive. After dedupe, row count drops by the number of discarded duplicates; you can verify by sorting the download on the key columns and confirming no adjacent identical keys remain under your chosen fields.

dedupe.heading: Duplicate logic on keys you choose
dedupe.text: Two rows are duplicates when every selected key column has identical text in each corresponding cell. Unselected columns do not affect the decision: a later row with the same id but an updated phone number still deletes if only id is in the key set and the id matches an earlier row. Exact match means no fuzzy deduplication by soundex, domain normalization, or trimmed whitespace unless the cells already match as stored. All-blank keys on multiple lines will collide if those columns are the sole keys, which may or may not be what you want for sparse data. Rows that differ in one key field by a single character count as distinct. For composite keys, partial overlap is insufficient; all chosen fields must match simultaneously.

dedupe.heading: CSV structure issues that affect deduplication
dedupe.text: Headers come from row one; if keys include misspelled header names from a bad export, pick the actual column labels shown in the tool. Delimiter errors can concatenate what should be two key fields into one, hiding duplicates or creating false uniqueness. Quoted fields keep embedded delimiters inside one value so "123,456" stays one id. Line endings from Windows or Unix are normalized by the parser but row order follows the sequence in the file as read, which defines which duplicate wins. If your policy is "keep latest by date", this tool always keeps first by position; you would sort the file appropriately before upload or adjust outside the browser. Skipped blank lines do not participate, so line numbers in a text editor may not match row indices in the preview.

dedupe.heading: Privacy, preview limits, and output shape
dedupe.text: Dedupe runs locally like the other CSV utilities on this site; files stay on your device. Output preserves all original columns for kept rows and drops entire duplicate lines rather than merging field values from duplicates into one row. No aggregate statistics are computed here. Preview capped at twelve rows is for layout inspection only; rely on download for reconciliation counts. Large files dedupe in memory; extremely wide or long sheets may require patience or preprocessing. Because processing is ephemeral, download the result before navigating away. The result file remains comma-separated text suitable for re-import elsewhere; encoding follows typical UTF-8 expectations for browser-generated downloads.

dedupe.heading: Confirming the right rows survived
dedupe.text: After download, sort by your key columns and scan for repeated keys; none should appear twice if keys were chosen correctly. Compare input and output record counts: their difference equals the number of rows removed. Check edge cases: first-row headers never dedupe against data. Single-row files pass through unchanged. If too many rows vanished, widen or narrow the key set—perhaps you keyed only on zip code when you needed address plus zip. If too few vanished, the selected key may contain extra distinguishing fields or casing splits what you consider one entity. Spot-check a known duplicate pair in the original against the output to confirm the earlier row’s non-key columns are the ones you wanted. Case-sensitive duplicates may need a normalization pass upstream before dedupe if policy requires it.

dedupe.heading: Typical dedupe scenarios and chaining tools
dedupe.text: Event registrations, newsletter signups, and lead dumps often need one row per email or per person id. Transaction logs might need dedupe on order id to remove accidental double posts while keeping legitimately repeated product lines on different orders when keyed differently. After dedupe, run the count tool on a status or region column to profile the cleaned set. Wide metrics sheets might unpivot before dedupe if uniqueness applies per id and metric name in long form rather than repeated wide columns. For migration, dedupe before loading a database unique index reduces constraint failures. Document which columns formed the key in your run notes so teammates reproduce the same rule. When business logic requires keeping the newest duplicate, pre-sort descending on a timestamp column in your editor, then dedupe so “first” in file equals newest.

unpivot.heading: How to unpivot a wide CSV to long format
unpivot.text: Upload a wide CSV, set delimiter, and confirm the header row. Designate one or more identifier columns that stay fixed on each output row, such as product id, store, or respondent id. Mark every column you want melted into values as unpivot targets; you need at least one identifier and at least one value column selected. All unselected columns are retained as identifiers. For each original data row, the tool emits one output row per selected value column, pairing the identifier cells with the column header name and the cell contents from that wide column. Blank cells in wide columns still produce a long row with an empty value field rather than skipping the combination. Preview shows up to twelve long rows; download includes the full unpivoted dataset with consistent long-form headers.

unpivot.heading: Worked example: quarterly sales columns
unpivot.text: Wide input headers: Store, Q1_Sales, Q2_Sales, Q3_Sales. One data row: Store "North", Q1_Sales "100", Q2_Sales "150", Q3_Sales blank. With Store as the only identifier and all three quarter columns selected, output has three rows: North, Q1_Sales, 100; North, Q2_Sales, 150; North, Q3_Sales, empty value cell. A second data row for Store "South" with values 80, 90, 70 adds three more lines. Identifiers repeat per melted column by design. If you selected only Q1 and Q2, Q3 would remain as an identifier column. Two identifier columns such as Store and Region would both repeat on each melted row. Row multiplication factor equals the number of selected value columns times the number of input data rows, which guides file size expectations before download.

unpivot.heading: Identifier columns versus attribute names
unpivot.text: Identifiers are dimensions you want repeated unchanged while each measure column fans out. Value column headers become entries in the attribute column of the long layout—often conceptually a variable name, period label, or question code. Cell text under each wide header becomes the value column entry without type coercion; numbers and dates remain text as in CSV. Selecting every non-id column unpivots the entire measure block; leaving descriptive static fields as identifiers keeps them on each long row for filtering later. Do not select the same column as both identifier and value. If two wide headers differ only by invisible whitespace, they produce two distinct attribute keys. Exact text rules apply: case and spaces in headers propagate to the long attribute field.

unpivot.heading: Delimiters, quotes, and empty wide cells
unpivot.text: Mis-set delimiters break wide headers so melted names look like garbage fragments. Quoted headers with commas inside become single attribute labels when parsed correctly. Empty trailing columns in some exports still unpivot if selected, yielding long rows with blank values. Completely empty input rows are skipped on import and contribute nothing. A wide cell that contains only spaces is that literal string in the value column, distinct from empty unless your source truly left the field null between delimiters. Pipe- or tab-separated wide tables follow the same unpivot rules once delimiter is set. Very wide sheets with dozens of month columns create proportionally many long rows per identifier; ensure downstream tools can handle the expanded row count. Header row must be first; extra preamble rows will mislabel identifiers.

unpivot.heading: Local unpivot, scale, and download behavior
unpivot.text: Unpivot executes in the browser without server upload. Memory use grows with input rows multiplied by selected value columns, so thousand-row files with hundreds of columns can become large long outputs. The preview of twelve rows helps verify attribute header naming and identifier repetition pattern before committing to a big download. Download delivers the complete long CSV, not preview-limited. No automatic aggregation or filtering runs after melt; one wide row always becomes exactly as many long rows as there are selected value columns unless you later dedupe or subset elsewhere. Session data clears when you leave unless saved. For regulated data, local melt avoids exposing wide extracts containing many attributes in one cloud pipeline step.

unpivot.heading: Checking long-format output
unpivot.text: Validate by picking one identifier from the preview and tracing it through each attribute row you expect from wide headers. Count long rows for one input line; it should equal the number of value columns ticked. Blank wide cells should appear as long rows with empty value fields if those columns were selected, confirming blanks were not dropped silently. Attribute names match the displayed column labels; empty or duplicate headers are renamed on import. Identifiers on all melted lines from the same source row must be identical across non-id fields. If row counts explode beyond expectation, you may have selected numeric id columns as values by mistake. If counts are too low, some wide columns may be unchecked or blank rows dominated import. Sort downloaded output by identifier then attribute to audit completeness against the wide source in a side-by-side review.

unpivot.heading: Why melt wide sheets and what to do after
unpivot.text: Charting and many databases prefer one observation per row with a metric name column instead of sprouting period columns. Survey exports with one column per question unpivot for per-question counts or filtering. Panel data with years across the header becomes panel-long for regression prep. After unpivot, use count on the attribute column to see which measures exist per file, or dedupe on identifier plus attribute if wide export accidentally duplicated keys when stacked. You may still need type casting or date parsing outside this tool because values stay text. For reverse needs, pivoting long to wide is a separate manual or spreadsheet operation. Save melted CSV before further transforms. When only a subset of periods matters, select those value columns only to avoid extra long rows. Chain dedupe first if wide rows were duplicate records before melt would duplicate the entire long block.
